unit.title: Cut, bend and install electrical conduits

summary: This unit teaches you to cut, bend and install the conduit that protects electrical cables. You will learn to choose PVC or steel conduit and its fittings, measure, cut, ream and thread it, make 90° bends, offsets and saddles in the right place by hand and with a bender, and fix the run straight, level and secure, with sound joints and earth continuity, ready for the cables to be drawn in.

blocks.p: **Conduit** is a tube that carries and protects electrical cables. It is fixed to the surface of walls and ceilings, or laid in block walls and concrete slabs as the building goes up. The cables are drawn in afterwards, so a conduit system can be rewired or added to later without breaking walls. In Jamaica most homes, schools, offices and shops are built of concrete block, and conduit is the usual way of wiring them.

This unit is for Level 2 trainees. It covers the conduit itself: choosing it, cutting, bending, joining and fixing it, and checking the finished run. Drawing the cables in and connecting them is covered in the wiring unit.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Work safely
Control sharp burrs, flying chips, solvent fumes, hot PVC, heavy lengths and drilling into walls; wear the right PPE.
Choose conduit and fittings
Tell PVC, thin-wall steel (EMT) and heavy-gauge steel apart, and choose the right couplings, boxes, bushes and saddles for the job and the place.
Measure, mark and cut
Measure twice from the drawing and the site, mark square and cut square with a hacksaw, pipe cutter or PVC cutter.
Ream and thread
Remove every burr, and thread heavy-gauge steel conduit with a die stock and cutting oil.
Bend conduit
Make 90° bends, kicks, offsets, saddles and back-to-back bends in PVC and steel, with no kinks or flattening.
Work out bends
Use the bender's take-up and marks and the offset and saddle rules, so each bend lands in the right place.
Join, fix and support
Make solvent-cement and screwed joints, fix boxes, and saddle the run straight, level and plumb at the right spacing.
Check and finish
Check earth continuity on steel runs, inspect the work against the drawing, leave a draw wire and clean up.

blocks.note: Concrete block walls and slabs mean much of Jamaica's conduit is cast in or chased in, and must be right first time: once the concrete is poured, a crushed or blocked conduit is very hard to put right. Surface conduit is common in workshops, warehouses, schools and in alterations to existing buildings. Near the coast, salt air rusts steel quickly, so PVC is widely used.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a conduit job from safety and choosing materials to the final check. The bend calculations are explained step by step with worked examples; practise them with a calculator. Your instructor will show you the benders, springs and dies used at the Centre and their own marks and charts.

head: Hazard
What can happen
Control
rows: Sharp cut ends and burrs
Deep cuts to hands; burrs that later cut cable insulation
Wear gloves when handling cut steel; ream and file every cut end at once
Flying chips and filings
Eye injuries when sawing, reaming, threading and drilling
Wear safety glasses
Hacksaw slipping
Cuts to the hand holding the work
Hold the conduit in a pipe vice, not by hand; start the cut gently with a thumb guiding the blade, then move the hand away
Solvent cement and primer
Fumes are harmful to breathe and can catch fire; the cement irritates skin and eyes
Good airflow, no smoking or flames nearby, close the tin after use, gloves, keep it off the skin
Heating PVC
Overheated or burnt PVC gives off harmful, choking fumes (hydrogen chloride) and can catch fire; hot PVC burns skin
Use a heat gun or heating box as the maker says, never a flame; heat evenly; gloves
Cutting oil
Skin irritation; slippery floors
Gloves, wipe up spills, wash hands after use
Long, heavy lengths
Back strain; hitting people, lights or windows with the ends
Lift correctly, get help with long lengths, watch both ends, carry them low
Bending steel
Back strain; a bender slipping; hands trapped
Firm, flat floor; foot on the pedal; steady pull; keep fingers clear of the shoe
Drilling walls for fixings
Drilling into hidden cables or pipes; dust; noise
Check with a detector first; safety glasses, dust mask and ear protection
Working at height
Falls from stepladders when fixing overhead runs
A sound stepladder or platform, set up correctly; do not over-reach

blocks.note: Never heat PVC with a blowtorch, lighter or open fire. A flame scorches the surface before the inside is soft, leaves weak spots, and the burning PVC gives off harmful fumes.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: If you are installing conduit in an existing building, the circuits near your route may be live. Check the drawings, use a detector, and have any circuit you might drill into isolated and locked off.

sections.title: Conduit types, fittings and choosing a system

head: Type
What it is
How it is joined
Notes
rows: Rigid PVC conduit
Plastic (polyvinyl chloride) tube; heavy-gauge and light-gauge grades
Solvent-cement couplings and fittings; adaptors to threaded entries
Light, cheap, does not rust, easy to cut. Bent cold with a spring or with heat. Gives no earth path. Grows and shrinks with temperature.
Thin-wall steel tubing (EMT, electrical metallic tubing)
Light galvanised steel tube, too thin to thread
Set-screw couplings and connectors (dry places) or compression ones (wet places)
Common for surface runs in commercial buildings. Bent with a hand bender.
Heavy-gauge (rigid) steel conduit
Thick-walled galvanised steel tube
Threaded at the ends for screwed couplings and box entries
Strongest protection; used where damage is likely and in industry. Heavy, slower to install, rusts at cut ends near the sea.
Flexible conduit (metal or plastic)
Spiral or corrugated flexible tube; a liquid-tight type has a plastic cover
Special connectors
Short final connections to motors, pumps and equipment that vibrates or must be moved.

blocks.p: Conduit is sold in trade sizes such as ½, ¾ and 1 inch, or metric sizes such as 20 mm and 25 mm, usually in lengths of about 3 m. Always check the size printed on the conduit against the drawing, and use fittings of the same system and size.

head: Fitting
Use
rows: Coupling
Joins two lengths in a straight line. An **expansion coupling** lets long PVC runs grow and shrink.
Adaptor
Joins PVC conduit to a threaded box entry or to another type of conduit.
Connector
Joins EMT or flexible conduit to a box.
Locknut and bush (bushing)
Hold a threaded conduit end in a box knockout. The bush also gives the cables a smooth edge.
Boxes: outlet, switch, junction and draw-in (pull) boxes
House accessories and joints, and give points to draw the cables in.
Inspection fittings: elbows, tees and conduit bodies with removable covers
Give access for drawing in and checking cables at a bend or junction.
Saddles and straps
Fix the conduit to the surface. A **spacer bar saddle** or distance saddle holds it a little off the wall.
End caps, stop ends and drain fittings
Close unused ends; let water out at the low points of outdoor runs.

head: Point
PVC conduit
Steel conduit
rows: Corrosion and salt air
Does not rust or corrode: the usual choice near the sea
Rusts, especially at cut ends and threads, even when galvanised
Strength
Can be cracked or crushed by heavy knocks
Strong; resists knocks and crushing
Heat and sun
Softens in strong heat; needs a sunlight-resistant grade outdoors
Not affected by normal heat or sun
Expansion
Grows about 0.06 mm per metre for every 1 °C rise
Grows only about a fifth as much
Earth path
None: a grounding (earth) conductor must always be drawn in
Can act as an earth path if every joint is tight; many specifications still ask for a separate earth conductor
Fire
Gives off harmful smoke if it burns
Does not burn
Work
Light, cheap, quick to cut and join
Heavier and slower; needs threading or compression fittings

ul: Read the drawing: the route, the box positions and heights, and any notes on conduit size and type.
Walk the route on site. Look for obstacles such as beams, pipes, windows and other services, and decide where bends, offsets and saddles are needed.
Mark level lines with a spirit level or laser level, vertical lines with a plumb bob or level, and long straight lines by **snapping a chalk line**.
Mark the box positions and the saddle positions on the wall.
**Measure twice, cut once.** A length cut short is waste.
Allow for the fittings: the depth the conduit goes into a coupling, adaptor or box.
Measure bends from the end or from the last bend, using the bender's marks (see the bend calculations section).
Mark the cut all the way round the conduit, with a marker or a wrap of tape, so the cut will be square.

blocks.p: Hold the conduit in a **pipe vice** (a chain vice or a yoke vice) close to the cut, so it cannot turn or move. Do not crush thin-wall steel or PVC in a flat-jawed bench vice.

ul: Fit the blade with the **teeth pointing away from the handle**, so it cuts on the push stroke, and tension it tight.
Choose the teeth to suit the wall: **at least three teeth should touch the wall at once**, or the teeth catch and strip. Fewer teeth per inch (TPI) cut thick walls faster; more TPI suit thin walls.
Start gently on the mark, then use steady, full-length strokes with light pressure, easing off on the return stroke.
Cut **square** (straight across), so the end sits fully home in couplings and boxes and the cables are not cut by a slanted edge.

head: Work
Typical blade
rows: Heavy-gauge steel conduit
18 or 24 TPI
Thin-wall steel (EMT)
24 or 32 TPI
PVC conduit
A fine-tooth hacksaw or junior hacksaw, or a PVC cutter

ul: **Pipe (tubing) cutter:** a sharp wheel turned round the tube gives a clean, square cut on steel, but rolls a heavy burr inside and narrows the end slightly, so the end must be reamed well.
**PVC cutter (ratchet shears):** gives a quick, clean, square cut on small PVC conduit without a saw.
Power saws are used only as the Centre's rules and the maker's instructions allow, with guards in place.

blocks.p: Every cut leaves a **burr**: a sharp, rough edge. The inside burr will cut the insulation of cables as they are drawn in, so it must be removed.

ul: Steel: remove the inside burr with a **conduit reamer** or a **half-round file**, and file the outside edge smooth.
PVC: remove the inside and outside burr with a deburring tool, a file or a knife used away from you.
Run your gloved finger or a cloth round the inside to check that it is smooth. Blow or wipe the filings out.

blocks.note: Ream every end straight after cutting, before the length goes anywhere. A burr found after the cables are in has already done its damage.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Heavy-gauge (rigid) steel conduit is joined with screwed couplings and threaded box entries, so its ends must be threaded on site. Thin-wall EMT is too thin to thread.

ul: A **die stock** (ratchet handle) and **dies** to match the conduit size and the thread type the fittings use
A **guide** that matches the outside of the conduit, so the die starts square
**Cutting oil** made for threading
A pipe vice, safety glasses and gloves

flow: Cut the end square and ream it
Hold the conduit firmly in the pipe vice, with a short length sticking out
Fit the die with its tapered (lead) side towards the conduit, and fit the guide
Oil the end of the conduit and the die
Push the die square onto the end and turn it clockwise with steady pressure until it bites
Keep turning, oiling often; every turn or so, turn back a little to break off the chips
Stop when the thread is long enough for the fitting to tighten fully
Turn the die off, clean off chips and oil
Check the thread by running a coupling on by hand
Paint the bare thread with zinc-rich paint

ul: **Why oil:** cutting oil cools and lubricates the die, gives a cleaner thread and makes the die last longer. Do not use water or grease.
**Why turn back:** turning back breaks the curls of metal (chips) so they do not jam the die and tear the thread.
**Thread length:** too short and the coupling or locknut will not tighten; too long and bare, unprotected thread is left showing.
**Why zinc-rich paint:** threading cuts through the galvanising, and the bare steel will rust, especially in Jamaica's humid and salty air.

head: Bend
What it is
Typical use
rows: 90° bend
A quarter turn
Turning a corner, such as from a wall up onto the ceiling, or a 'stub-up' rising from a floor
Kick
A single bend of less than 90°
Moving the run away from a surface, or lining it up with a box
Offset (set)
Two equal bends in opposite directions that step the run to one side and back to parallel
Passing a step in the wall, a beam edge, or entering a box that stands off the wall
Saddle
Three bends (a three-bend saddle) or four bends (two offsets) that take the run over an obstacle and back to its line
Crossing a pipe or another conduit
Back-to-back bend
Two 90° bends on one length, making a U shape
Running down a wall, across, and back up; or round a beam

blocks.p: All the bends on one length must lie in the **same flat plane** unless the drawing needs otherwise. A length with its bends twisted out of line (a 'dog-leg') will not lie flat against the wall.

flow: Choose the bending spring made for that size and type of conduit, and tie a cord to its end
Mark the bend position on the conduit
Push the spring in until its middle is at the bend mark
Bend slowly over your knee or a rounded former, spreading the bend so it is smooth
Bend a little past the angle you want, then ease it back
Check the angle with a square or a level
Twist the spring in the direction that tightens its coils, so it gets thinner, and pull it out with the cord

ul: The spring supports the wall of the conduit from inside, so it does not **flatten or kink**.
PVC springs back a little when released, which is why you bend slightly past the angle and ease back.
In Jamaica's warm weather, 20 mm and 25 mm PVC usually bends cold. In a cool, air-conditioned room it may need gentle warming first.

blocks.p: Larger PVC conduit, and sharper bends, are made with heat. Use a **heating box** (hot box) or a **heat gun**, as the maker says. Heat the whole length of the bend evenly, turning the conduit all the time, until it is soft and flexible but not scorched. Bend it over a former or by hand, hold it at the angle, and let it cool (a damp cloth speeds this) so it sets. Brown marks, bubbles or a smell of burning mean it is overheated: cut that piece out.

ul: **Hand bender:** a curved shoe (former) on a long handle. Put the conduit in the shoe on a firm, flat floor, line the mark up with the bender's mark, put your foot on the foot pedal to hold the conduit in the shoe, and pull the handle with steady pressure, keeping the conduit flat on the floor.
**Bending machine:** for heavier conduit, the conduit is pulled round a curved **former** (shoe) by a lever, held by a back guide or roller.
Use a bender or former that matches the size of the conduit. The wrong size flattens or kinks the tube.

head: Fault
Cause
What to do
rows: Kink or flattened outside of the bend
Bent too sharply, wrong size of bender or spring, spring not at the bend, or bent in one jerk
Cut it out and make the bend again: a kink reduces the space for cables and can damage them
Wrinkles on the inside of the bend
Wrong bender, or the conduit was not held in the shoe
Cut it out and bend again
Dog-leg (bends twisted out of plane)
The conduit was turned in the bender between bends
Correct it if the bender allows, or remake it
Bend in the wrong place
Wrong measurement, take-up or mark used
Remake it; check your measurements and marks
Scorched PVC
Too much heat, or a flame
Cut it out; use even heat from a heat gun or box

blocks.note: Never hammer a kinked bend back into shape or cover a dent with tape. The damage is still inside, where the cables will catch on it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A bend uses up length and must land in the right place on the run. Benders and bending charts make this easy, as long as you use the right figure for the right bend. The figures below are the usual rules; always check them against your own bender's marks and chart.

A 90° bend does not start exactly at the mark: part of the length goes round the shoe. The **take-up** is the amount you take off the height you want, so the back of the bend lands in the right place. It is printed on most hand benders; a common figure is about **125 mm (5 inches) for a ½-inch EMT bender**, about 150 mm for ¾ inch and about 200 mm for 1 inch.

**Worked example.** You need a stub-up 300 mm high in ½-inch EMT. Take-up 125 mm. Mark the conduit at 300 − 125 = **175 mm** from the end. Line the mark up with the bender's arrow (start mark), with the end of the conduit pointing the way the bender's instructions show, and bend to 90°. Measure from the floor to the back of the bend to check: 300 mm.

blocks.note: Most hand benders carry an arrow for the start of a stub-up, a mark (often a star) for the back of a 90° bend, and a notch or teardrop for the centre of a saddle. Learn the marks on the bender you use.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: For an offset made with two equal bends, the distance between the two bend marks = **offset depth × multiplier**. Smaller angles need the bends further apart, but give a gentler path that is easier to pull cables through.
**Worked example.** A run must step out 150 mm to pass a wall projection, using two 30° bends. Distance between marks = 150 × 2 = **300 mm**.

An offset moves the run sideways, so the conduit no longer travels its full length along the wall: the run gets shorter. This loss of length is the **shrink**. Shrink = offset depth × the shrink figure in the table. For the 150 mm offset with 30° bends: 150 × 0.27 ≈ **40 mm**. When you measure from the end of the conduit towards an obstacle, add the shrink to the measurement for the first mark, or the offset will finish short of where you need it.

A common three-bend saddle uses a **45° centre bend and two 22½° outer bends**. A common rule is: the outer marks are **2.5 × the height of the obstacle** from the centre mark, one on each side, and the shrink is about **0.19 × the height**.

**Worked example.** A pipe stands 40 mm off the wall. Outer marks: 2.5 × 40 = **100 mm** each side of the centre mark. Shrink: 0.19 × 40 ≈ 8 mm, so mark the centre bend 8 mm further from the end than the measured centre of the pipe. Make the centre bend first so it sits over the pipe, then the two outer bends in the opposite direction, all in the same plane. Check against the pipe and with a level before fixing.
A **four-bend saddle** is two offsets: one to rise over the obstacle and one to come back down, with the straight between them long enough to clear it.

After the first 90° bend, measure from the **back** of that bend to where the back of the second bend must be, mark it, and line the mark up with the bender's back-of-bend mark, with the bender facing the other way. Check the measurement between the backs of the two bends after bending.

blocks.h: How much bending between draw-in points

blocks.p: Every bend makes it harder to pull cables in. The NEC allows no more than **360° of bends in total** between draw-in points (pull points), for example four 90° bends. Many installers, and British practice, put a draw-in box or inspection fitting after two 90° bends. Count the offsets and saddles too: a 30° offset is 60° of bending. If the run needs more, add a draw-in box or an inspection fitting.

flow: Cut square and deburr the end
Check the conduit and the fitting's socket are clean and dry
Dry-fit to check the length and the line
Brush cement evenly on the outside of the conduit end and the inside of the socket
Push the conduit fully home with a slight twist, at once
Hold it for a few seconds while it grips
Wipe off any extra cement
Let the joint set before it takes any strain

ul: Use the cement made for PVC conduit, and a primer only if the maker says so.
In hot weather the solvent evaporates quickly and the cement sets fast: work quickly and push the joint home at once. In damp weather full curing takes longer.
Close the tin after use, keep it away from heat and flames, and work where there is good airflow.

blocks.p: PVC conduit grows as it warms and shrinks as it cools: about **0.06 mm per metre for every 1 °C** change. A surface run in the Jamaican sun can easily change by 30 to 40 °C between a cool night and a hot afternoon.

**Worked example.** A 15 m PVC run on a sunny wall changes by 40 °C. Movement = 15 × 40 × 0.06 = **36 mm**. That is enough to buckle the run between its fixings or pull it out of a box. The NEC calls for an **expansion coupling** wherever the expected movement is 6 mm or more. Fit it as the maker says, with the saddles holding the conduit snugly but not so tight that it cannot slide.

ul: **Heavy-gauge steel:** screwed couplings and box entries, tightened fully with the threads fully engaged, so the run is mechanically strong and electrically continuous.
**EMT:** set-screw couplings and connectors in dry places; **compression** (raintight) couplings and connectors in wet places and outdoors. Tighten set screws and compression nuts firmly.

**At steel boxes:** the threaded end or connector goes through the knockout with a **locknut** tightened so it bites into the box, and a **bush** on the end inside, so the cables pass over a smooth, rounded edge.

blocks.p: Remove only the knockouts you need. Spare knockouts are left closed to keep out dust, insects and fingers; an opened knockout that is not used is closed with a blanking plug.

ul: Fit a saddle **close to each box, bend and fitting**, then space the others **evenly** along the straight runs at the spacing the drawing and code give.

As a guide, the NEC asks for small rigid PVC conduit (½ to 1 inch) to be supported at least every **900 mm**, and EMT and steel conduit within **900 mm of every box or fitting** and at least every **3 m**. Many drawings ask for closer spacing on surface work for a neat finish.
On concrete block, drill with a **masonry bit** of the size the wall plug needs, in a hammer drill, and fix the saddles with **screws into wall plugs**. Never nail into mortar joints or rely on glue.
Check for hidden cables and pipes with a detector before drilling. Wear safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection.
Use **spacer bar saddles** or distance saddles where the conduit must stand a little off the wall, for example on uneven or damp walls or to match box entries.
Check the run with a spirit level: horizontal runs **level**, vertical drops **plumb**, all parallel to the walls and ceiling.
Use weatherproof boxes and fittings with their gaskets, and compression fittings on EMT.
Avoid **water traps**: low points where water collects. Arrange the run to drain, and fit a drain fitting at a low point if needed.
Use PVC rated for sunlight outdoors, and allow for expansion.
Seal where a conduit passes from outside into the building, so rain and insects cannot follow it in.
Conductors in outdoor conduit must be rated for wet places, because condensation forms inside.

blocks.p: Use a short length of **flexible conduit** (liquid-tight where wet) for the final connection to a motor, pump or other equipment that vibrates or has to be moved for adjustment. Rigid conduit fixed straight to a vibrating motor can crack or work its joints loose.

A steel conduit system can carry fault current back to the panel, but only if every coupling, connector, locknut and box joint is tight and clean. A loose joint has a high resistance, so in a fault the conduit can become live and the breaker may not trip.

ul: Tighten every joint fully, and fit locknuts so they bite through the paint or galvanising.
Use **earth tags** or bonding where the drawing shows them, for example across flexible conduit.
PVC gives no earth path at all: a **grounding (earth) conductor** is always drawn in with the circuit cables. Many specifications, and the code for some circuits, require one in steel conduit too.

blocks.p: With everything dead and no supply connected, test the run from box to box with a **low-resistance ohmmeter** (or a multimeter on its lowest resistance range), after nulling or noting the resistance of the test leads. A good run gives a **low, steady** reading, usually a fraction of an ohm for a short run. A high reading, or one that jumps about when the conduit is moved, points to a loose or dirty joint. Record the reading.

head: Check
What good work looks like
rows: Against the drawing
Route, boxes and fittings in the right places and at the right heights
Line
Runs straight, level and plumb, parallel to walls and ceiling
Bends
Smooth, no kinks, flattening or wrinkles, all in one plane, landing in the right place
Cut ends
Square and reamed, with no burrs inside
Joints
Couplings tight and fully home; PVC joints fully cemented; locknuts and bushes at every steel box
Fixings
Saddles near every box, bend and fitting and evenly along runs; nothing loose
Access
Draw-in boxes and inspection fittings where needed; covers available
Bending between draw-in points
Not more than the code allows
Outdoors
Weatherproof fittings, expansion couplings, no water traps
Capacity
Conduit size suits the cables to be drawn in: under the NEC, three or more conductors may fill no more than 40% of the conduit's area

blocks.p: Report and correct any fault before the cables go in.

ul: Pull a **draw wire** or draw cord through each finished run and leave it in, tied off at both ends, so the cables can be pulled in later.
Fit covers or temporary caps to boxes and fittings to keep out plaster, dust and water.
Collect steel off-cuts and filings for recycling or the scrap bin, and PVC off-cuts and shavings for the waste bin. Leave nothing in ceilings or on the floor.
Close and store solvent cement and cutting oil; dispose of empty tins and oily rags as the Centre directs.
Clean and return the benders, springs, dies and tools; report any damage, such as a worn die or a stretched spring.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the hazards of cutting, threading, bending and fixing conduit and control each one.
I can explain why PVC must never be heated with a flame, and why solvent cement needs good airflow.
I can tell PVC, EMT, heavy-gauge steel and flexible conduit apart and say how each is joined.
I can choose between PVC and steel for a job, including near the sea.
I can name the common fittings and say what each is for.
I can mark out a route with a level, plumb bob and chalk line, and measure twice allowing for fittings.
I can fit a hacksaw blade correctly, choose the teeth, and cut square.
I can ream and deburr every cut end.
I can thread heavy-gauge conduit with a die stock and cutting oil and protect the thread.
I can bend PVC with a spring and with heat, and steel with a hand bender, without kinks.
I can use take-up to place a 90° bend, and work out the spacing and shrink of an offset.
I can mark out a three-bend saddle and a back-to-back bend.
I can count the bending between draw-in points and add a draw-in point when needed.
I can make solvent-cement and screwed joints and fit locknuts and bushes.
I can work out PVC expansion and fit an expansion coupling.
I can fix saddles at the right spacing and check a run is level and plumb.
I can check the earth continuity of a steel run and inspect a finished installation.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: At least 3 teeth
Should touch the wall at once when sawing
About 125 mm (5 in)
A common take-up for a ½-inch EMT hand bender; check your bender
Offset multipliers for 30° / 45° / 22½° bends
About 0.27 × depth
Shrink for a 30° offset
2.5 × height
Distance from the centre mark to each outer mark of a 45°/22½° three-bend saddle
Most bending allowed between draw-in points (NEC)
About 0.06 mm per m per °C
Expansion of PVC conduit
900 mm and 3 m
NEC support spacing: EMT and steel within 900 mm of boxes and every 3 m; small PVC every 900 mm
Most of a conduit's area that three or more conductors may fill (NEC)

terms: Back-to-back bend
Two 90° bends on one length, making a U shape.
Bending spring
A steel spring pushed inside PVC conduit to stop it flattening while it is bent.
Burr
The sharp, rough edge left on a conduit after it is cut.
Chalk line
A string coated in chalk, snapped against a wall to mark a long straight line.
Coupling
A fitting that joins two lengths of conduit in a straight line.
Die stock
The handle that holds a die for cutting threads on conduit.
Draw-in point
A box or inspection fitting from which cables are pulled into the conduit.
EMT
Electrical metallic tubing: thin-wall steel conduit joined with set-screw or compression fittings.
Expansion coupling
A fitting that lets a PVC run grow and shrink with temperature.
Former (shoe)
The curved part of a bender that the conduit is bent around.
Kick
A single bend of less than 90°.
Locknut and bush
The nut and rounded fitting that hold a threaded conduit in a box knockout.
Offset (set)
Two equal bends that step a run to one side and back to parallel.
Pipe vice
A vice that holds round conduit firmly for cutting and threading.
PVC
Polyvinyl chloride: the plastic used for non-metallic conduit.
Reaming
Removing the burr from the inside of a cut conduit end.
Saddle (bend)
Bends that take a run over an obstacle and back to its line.
Saddle (fixing)
A strap that fixes conduit to a surface; a spacer bar saddle holds it off the wall.
Shrink
The length lost along a run when an offset or saddle is made in it.
Take-up
The length taken off the wanted height so that a 90° bend lands in the right place.
TPI
Teeth per inch: a measure of how fine a saw blade is.

c1.title: Surface PVC at a Treasure Beach restaurant
c1.text: Electrician Mr Marlon Barrett and trainee Keisha Stewart are running surface PVC conduit along the sea-facing wall of a restaurant in Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth. One straight run is 24 m long and gets the full afternoon sun; the owner says the wall is cool at night and very hot by 3 p.m. The wall is concrete block. It is 33 °C at midday when they start making the solvent-cement joints.

c2.title: EMT in a Kingston warehouse
c2.text: Trainee Andre Palmer is helping electrician Ms Simone Richards run ¾-inch EMT along a warehouse wall on Spanish Town Road, Kingston. The run must step out 150 mm to pass a concrete ledge, and at the far end it rises as a 450 mm stub-up into a panel. Her hand bender has a take-up of 150 mm for ¾-inch EMT. She cuts the EMT with a tubing cutter. Part of the run passes the open loading door, where rain blows in.

c3.title: Heavy-gauge steel at a Lucea pumping station
c3.text: At a water pumping station near Lucea, Hanover, trainee Christopher Barnes is working with an electrician on a run of heavy-gauge galvanised steel conduit from a starter panel to a pump motor. He is threading the conduit ends with a die stock. On the way, the run must cross a pipe that stands 60 mm off the wall, using a three-bend saddle with a 45° centre bend and two 22½° outer bends. The route already has four 90° bends between the panel and the motor's terminal box.

c4.title: Spring bends at the St Ann's Bay workshop
c4.text: At the Centre's workshop in St Ann's Bay, trainee Jodian Wright is practising 90° bends in 20 mm PVC conduit with a bending spring while her instructor, Mr Courtney Daley, watches. Her first bend has a kink. Her second springs back to about 80° when she lets go. On her third, the spring sticks inside when she tries to pull it out. Later Mr Daley lets her try a heat gun on a length of 25 mm conduit.

questions.q: What must the PVC conduit and fittings for this wall be suitable for?
o: Being painted with oil-based paint
Long exposure to strong sunlight
Carrying the earth current itself
Threading with a die stock on site
questions.why: Ordinary PVC breaks down and becomes brittle in years of strong sun, so outdoor runs need conduit and fittings rated as sunlight-resistant. PVC is never an earth path, and it is not threaded.

questions.q: If the 24 m run warms by about 35 °C, how much could it grow, at about 0.06 mm per metre per °C?
o: About 2 mm
About 5 mm
About 50 mm
About 500 mm
questions.why: Movement = length × temperature change × 0.06 = 24 × 35 × 0.06 ≈ 50 mm. That is far more than the 6 mm at which an expansion coupling is needed.

questions.q: With an expansion coupling fitted, how should the saddles hold the conduit?
o: Snugly, but free enough for the conduit to slide
As tight as possible, so the run cannot move at all
Loosely, with a saddle only at each end of the run
Glued to the conduit, so they move together with it
questions.why: The expansion coupling can only take up the movement if the conduit can slide through its saddles. Clamped tight, the run buckles or pulls out of its fittings; with too few saddles it sags.

questions.q: How does the 33 °C heat affect the solvent-cement joints?
o: The cement sets more slowly, so wait before pushing in
It sets faster, so push each joint home at once
Heat makes the cement unnecessary on outdoor joints
Warm the joint first with a flame to help the cement
questions.why: In heat the solvent evaporates quickly, so the cement grips sooner. Apply it and push the conduit fully home straight away, with a slight twist, then hold it. Never use a flame near PVC or solvent cement.

questions.q: Ms Richards wants two 45° bends for the 150 mm offset. About how far apart should Andre mark them?
o: About 150 mm
About 300 mm
About 390 mm
About 210 mm
questions.why: Distance between bends = depth × multiplier. For 45° the multiplier is about 1.4: 150 × 1.4 = 210 mm. 300 mm would suit 30° bends, and 390 mm 22½° bends.

questions.q: Andre measures from the end of the EMT to the ledge. For the 45° offset, about how much shrink should he allow?
o: About 60 mm
About 15 mm
About 210 mm
About 150 mm
questions.why: Shrink = depth × the shrink figure for the angle: about 0.41 for 45°, so 150 × 0.41 ≈ 60 mm. Adding it to the measurement makes the offset finish where it is needed, not 60 mm short.

questions.q: For the 450 mm stub-up with a take-up of 150 mm, where should Andre put the mark?
o: 600 mm from the end
450 mm from the end
300 mm from the end
150 mm from the end
questions.why: Take the take-up off the height wanted: 450 − 150 = 300 mm. Line that mark up with the bender's start arrow, and the back of the finished bend will be 450 mm from the end.

questions.q: The tubing cutter leaves a raised ridge inside each cut end. What should Andre do?
o: Leave it, as the cable sheath will smooth it
Fold it flat with pliers so it lies down
Ream it smooth before the length is fitted
Cover it with tape inside the conduit end
questions.why: A tubing cutter rolls a heavy burr inside the end, which would cut the insulation of every cable drawn past it. Ream it away with a reamer or half-round file, and check by feel.

questions.q: Which couplings suit the length of EMT by the open loading door?
o: Set-screw couplings, tightened well
Solvent-cement couplings, as on PVC
Compression couplings for wet places
Threaded couplings with a die-cut thread
questions.why: Compression couplings and connectors seal against rain and are used on EMT in wet places. Set-screw types are for dry places only. EMT is too thin to thread, and solvent cement is for PVC.

questions.q: Using the 2.5 × height rule, how far from the centre mark should Christopher mark each outer bend?
o: 60 mm
150 mm
120 mm
240 mm
questions.why: For a 45° centre bend with 22½° outer bends, each outer mark is 2.5 × the obstacle height from the centre mark: 2.5 × 60 = 150 mm, one on each side.

questions.q: Which way round should the die be fitted in the die stock?
o: With its tapered lead side facing the conduit
With its flat back face against the conduit
Either way, as both faces of a die are the same
With the guide removed so it starts more easily
questions.why: The tapered lead side lets the die start cutting gradually and square. Fitted backwards, the die will not bite properly and can cut a ragged, crooked thread. The guide keeps it square.

questions.q: The saddle adds more bending to a route that already has four 90° bends. What should be done?
o: Pull the cables extra hard to get round
Leave out the saddle and cut the pipe instead
Make all the bends sharper to save length
Add a draw-in box or inspection fitting
questions.why: Four 90° bends already reach the 360° allowed between draw-in points; the saddle adds about 90° more. A draw-in box or inspection fitting splits the run, so the cables can be pulled in without damage.

questions.q: Why should the last short length into the pump motor's terminal box be flexible conduit?
o: Flexible conduit is cheaper than rigid steel
It takes the motor's vibration and adjustment
It gives a better earth path than rigid steel
It is easier to thread than rigid conduit
questions.why: A motor vibrates and may be moved to adjust its belt or alignment. A short flexible (liquid-tight in wet places) length takes this movement; rigid conduit would crack or work loose. Flexible conduit is a poorer earth path, not a better one.

questions.q: What most likely caused the kink in Jodian's first bend?
o: She bent the conduit slowly and evenly
She bent it past 90° and eased it back
The conduit was too warm from the room
The spring was not at the bend mark
questions.why: The spring supports the wall only where it is. If its middle is not at the bend, the unsupported wall flattens and kinks. Bending slowly and easing back from just past the angle are correct methods.

questions.q: How should Jodian check that a bend is exactly 90°?
o: Look along it from the end of the length
Measure the length of the bend with a tape
Compare it with the bend on the drawing
Use a try square or a level's corner
questions.why: A try square, or the corner of a level, shows at once whether the two legs are at right angles. Judging by eye or from a drawing is not accurate enough for a run that must sit flat and square.

questions.q: How should the stuck spring be freed?
o: Twist it tighter, then pull it out
Heat the bend so the PVC lets go of it
Grip the end with pliers and pull hard
Leave it inside and use another spring
questions.why: Twisting the spring in the direction that winds its coils tighter makes it thinner, so it slides out on its cord. Heating or yanking it can damage the bend or stretch the spring.

questions.q: Which is the right way for Jodian to use the heat gun on the 25 mm conduit?
o: Hold it close on one spot until it browns
Heat only the inside of the bend position
Warm the bend length evenly, turning it
Use a lighter as well to speed it up
questions.why: Heat the whole length of the bend evenly, turning the conduit, until it is soft. Heating one spot scorches it, gives off harmful fumes and makes a weak, kinked bend. Never use a flame.

questions.q: Which hacksaw blade is the best choice for cutting thin-wall EMT?
o: 10 TPI
14 TPI
18 TPI
32 TPI
questions.why: A thin wall needs fine teeth, so that at least three teeth are on the wall at once. 24 or 32 TPI suits thin-wall tube; coarse blades catch on the wall and strip their teeth.

questions.q: Under the NEC, how close to each box must an EMT run be supported?
o: Within 900 mm of the box
Within 3 m of the box
Within 1.5 m of the box
No support is needed near a box
questions.why: EMT is fixed within 900 mm of every box or fitting, and at least every 3 m along the run. Saddles near boxes and bends stop the conduit being levered out of its fittings.

questions.q: A low-resistance ohmmeter reads a steady 0.2 Ω on one steel run, and jumps between 3 Ω and 40 Ω on another. What does the second reading suggest?
o: The ohmmeter needs a new battery fitted
A loose or dirty joint somewhere on the run
That run is longer, so it reads much higher
A good earth path, as higher means safer
questions.why: A sound steel run gives a low, steady reading. A high reading that changes as the conduit moves points to a loose coupling, connector or locknut, which must be found and tightened before the run is relied on as an earth path.
